hook: Two people sit side by side on the same flight. One paid \$90 because she booked a month ahead; the other paid \$260 because he booked yesterday. The seat cost the airline the same. Why would a seller charge two prices for one product, and who wins?

ideas: Price discrimination: selling the same good at different prices to different buyers, for reasons other than cost.
Three conditions: market power, a way to sort buyers by elasticity, and a way to stop resale.
The less elastic group pays the higher price; the more elastic group pays less.
Perfect price discrimination: each buyer pays the most they will pay. MR = D, so Q is where D = MC: no deadweight loss, no consumer surplus, all surplus is profit.

misconception.wrong: Perfect price discrimination makes consumers better off, because it removes the deadweight loss.
misconception.right: The deadweight loss disappears, so total surplus is as large as it can be, but every bit of it goes to the firm: consumer surplus falls to zero. Efficiency and fairness are different questions.

summary: Price discrimination is charging different buyers different prices for the same good when costs do not differ. It needs market power, a way to sort buyers and a way to stop resale, and it charges the higher price to the less elastic group. It raises the firm's profit and usually its output. With perfect price discrimination, each buyer pays the most they will pay, so the MR curve is the demand curve and the firm produces where demand meets MC: the efficient quantity, with no deadweight loss and no consumer surplus.
